title: Implementing End-to-End Security Controls for Cloud and AI Workloads

modules.title: Manage identity, access and governance
modules.intro: Every cloud control starts with who can sign in, what secrets apps use, and which rules keep resources in line (about 20 to 25 percent of the exam). Meet **Brightwater Insurance**, an 800 person insurer that runs claims processing on Azure: a customer portal on App Service, claim photos in Storage, a policy database in Azure SQL, containers on AKS and a claims assistant agent built in Microsoft Foundry. Tomasi, its cloud security engineer, has to secure all of it, starting with identity and governance.

lessons.title: Privileged Identity Management
steps: Standing privilege is the risk

If a permanent Global Administrator or subscription Owner is phished, the attacker has everything. **Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** replaces standing rights with **just in time** and **time bound** access.
Eligible and active

An **eligible** assignment holds no permissions until the user **activates** it, often with MFA, a reason and approval. An **active** assignment works immediately but can still have an end date. PIM covers Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles such as Owner on a subscription, and PIM for Groups.
Role settings

Each role's settings set the longest activation (1 to 24 hours), require MFA or a Conditional Access **authentication context** (to demand phishing resistant MFA or a compliant device), justification, ticket information and **approval**. For Azure resources, settings are per role and per scope.
Licensing and management

PIM needs Entra ID P2 or ID Governance for users with eligible or time bound assignments. Privileged Role Administrator manages PIM for Entra roles, and Owner or User Access Administrator manages it for Azure resources. Tomasi makes the platform team eligible for Contributor on the claims subscription for four hours with approval.

check.q: Brightwater's platform engineers need Contributor on production only during change windows. How should Tomasi assign it?
options: Eligible Contributor in PIM with approval
check.why: An eligible assignment means no rights until activation, and approval adds a second check for production. Permanent active and Owner both give standing access, and a dynamic group still grants rights all the time.

lessons.key: PIM makes privileged roles just in time: eligible users activate for a limited time with MFA, authentication context, reasons or approval.

lessons.title: Conditional Access policies
steps: If, then

A **Conditional Access** policy is an if then rule checked after the first sign in step. The if part names **users** (always excluding emergency access accounts), **target resources** and **conditions** such as risk, device platform, location and client app. The then part blocks or grants access with requirements. It needs Entra ID P1.
Grant requirements

Grant controls include MFA, an **authentication strength** (such as phishing resistant MFA), a compliant or hybrid joined device, an app protection policy and a password change. Every matching policy applies, all requirements must be met, and **block always wins**.
Deploying safely

**Report only** mode evaluates policies on real sign ins without enforcing them, **What If** simulates a sign in, and the insights workbook shows the impact over time once logs reach a Log Analytics workspace.
Session controls and a baseline

Session controls set sign in frequency, persistent browser sessions, app enforced restrictions, Defender for Cloud Apps session control and token protection. Tomasi's baseline: phishing resistant strength for admin roles, block legacy authentication, and MFA for Azure management.

check.q: Two policies apply to a Brightwater admin: one grants access with MFA, the other blocks access from outside New Zealand. She signs in from Fiji. What happens?
options: She is let in once she completes MFA
The policy created most recently decides
She gets a limited, browser only session
check.why: All matching policies apply and a block overrides any grant. Completing MFA cannot lift a block, and policy age has no effect on evaluation.

lessons.key: Conditional Access combines users, resources and conditions into block or grant decisions, all matching policies apply, and block wins.

lessons.title: Authentication methods, MFA and passwordless
steps: One methods policy

Methods are managed in the **authentication methods policy**, targeting each method to users or groups. Older tenants migrate away from the legacy MFA and SSPR method settings. **Authentication Policy Administrator** configures the policy.
Common methods

**Microsoft Authenticator** offers push with **number matching**, passwordless phone sign in and passkeys. A **Temporary Access Pass** is a time limited code for onboarding or recovery. Text and voice are the weakest and best kept as fallbacks. OATH tokens offer one time codes.
Passwordless and phishing resistant

**Passkeys (FIDO2)**, **Windows Hello for Business** and multifactor **certificate based authentication** are phishing resistant, because the key only works with the genuine site. Passkey profiles can restrict passkey types, enforce attestation and allow or block specific key models.
Enforcing strength

Conditional Access **require authentication strength** with phishing resistant MFA enforces those methods. Users must have done MFA in the last five minutes to register a passkey, and a TAP satisfies that for new staff. Brightwater gives every admin a FIDO2 key.

check.q: Tomasi wants Brightwater admins to use only methods that a fake login page cannot reuse. What should he require?
options: Text message codes with a short expiry
check.why: Phishing resistant strength allows only FIDO2 passkeys, Windows Hello for Business and multifactor CBA. Push with number matching and text codes can still be relayed by a phishing site, and plain MFA accepts those weaker methods.

lessons.key: Manage methods in one policy, and enforce passkeys, Windows Hello or certificate auth with a phishing resistant authentication strength.

lessons.title: Identity for applications
steps: Two objects per app

An **app registration** (the application object) lives in the home tenant and defines the app: client ID, redirect addresses, credentials, permissions it asks for and app roles. An **enterprise application** (the service principal) is the app's instance in each tenant that uses it, holding consented permissions, assignments and SSO settings.
Enterprise app properties

**Assignment required** set to yes means only assigned users or groups get tokens. **Visible to users** only controls My Apps. **Enabled for users to sign in** is the kill switch. Application Administrator and Cloud Application Administrator manage apps, and Application Developer can register them.
Credentials

Apps prove who they are with a **client secret** (easy but leak prone), a **certificate** (recommended, ideally kept in Key Vault) or a **federated identity credential**, which trusts tokens from GitHub Actions, Kubernetes or another cloud so no secret exists at all. Application management policies can limit secret lifetimes or block secrets.
Workload ID Premium

**Microsoft Entra Workload ID Premium** adds Conditional Access for workload identities, such as blocking a service principal outside known IP ranges, ID Protection for risky service principals and access reviews for privileged service principals. Brightwater's deployment pipeline uses a federated credential, so there is no secret to steal.

check.q: Brightwater's GitHub Actions pipeline deploys to Azure. Tomasi wants no stored secret for it at all. What should the app registration use?
check.why: Workload identity federation lets Entra ID trust GitHub's tokens, so no secret exists to leak. Rotated secrets and stored certificates still exist somewhere, and user accounts are for people.

lessons.key: App registrations define an app, enterprise apps are its per tenant instance, and federated credentials or certificates beat client secrets.

lessons.title: OAuth permission grants and consent
steps: Delegated and application permissions

**Delegated** permissions let an app act as the signed in user and never exceed that user's rights. **Application** permissions let it act as itself with no user, often across the whole tenant, and always need **admin consent**.
What consent creates
Consent creates a **permission grant** on the app's service principal. Admin consent grants on behalf of everyone. Grants can be reviewed and revoked on the enterprise app's permissions page.
User consent settings

Options are: do not allow user consent; allow it for **verified publishers** and only for permissions classified as **low impact** (recommended); or allow it for any app, the risky legacy setting. Permission classifications decide what counts as low impact.
The attack and the workflow

**Illicit consent grant**, or consent phishing, tricks users into granting a malicious app access to their mail or files. The **admin consent workflow** lets users request consent with a reason, reviewed by chosen people who already hold a role able to grant it. Tomasi finds and revokes a grant a claims handler gave to an unknown PDF tool.

check.q: A Brightwater user was tricked into granting an unknown app permission to read her mail. What should Tomasi do first?
options: Block the user from signing in
Turn off user consent for the future only
check.why: Removing the grant on the service principal stops the app using it now. The malicious app's own secret belongs to the attacker, blocking the user does not remove the app's existing access, and changing consent settings affects only future requests.

lessons.key: Application permissions always need admin consent, limit user consent to verified publishers and low impact permissions, and revoke illicit grants.

lessons.title: Managed identities
steps: Identity without secrets

A **managed identity** is a service principal whose credentials Azure creates and rotates. Code on the resource asks for a token through the Azure Identity library or the local metadata endpoint, then uses it with Key Vault, Storage, SQL or Azure Resource Manager.
System assigned
A **system assigned** identity is enabled on one resource, shares its name, is deleted automatically with it, and cannot be shared with any other resource.
User assigned

A **user assigned** identity is its own Azure resource that can be attached to many resources and must be deleted on its own. It suits scale sets, resources rebuilt often and granting access before deployment. **Managed Identity Contributor** creates them and **Managed Identity Operator** attaches them.
Authorisation is separate

Turning on an identity grants nothing. Tomasi gives the claims portal's identity **Key Vault Secrets User** on its vault and Storage Blob Data Reader on the photos container. Without those role assignments, token requests succeed but calls are refused.

check.q: Brightwater rebuilds its VM scale set weekly, and every instance needs the same Key Vault access. Which identity type fits best?
options: A system assigned identity on each VM
A client secret stored in each image
A service principal with a certificate
check.why: A user assigned identity survives rebuilds and keeps its role assignments. System assigned identities are recreated with each resource, and secrets or certificates reintroduce credentials to manage.

lessons.key: Managed identities remove secrets, system assigned ones live with one resource, user assigned ones are shared, and both still need role assignments.

lessons.title: Deploying and configuring Key Vault
steps: Tiers

**Azure Key Vault** stores secrets, keys and certificates. **Standard** uses software protected keys. **Premium** adds HSM protected keys. **Managed HSM** is a dedicated single tenant HSM cluster with its own security domain and local RBAC, holding keys only.
Design choices

One vault per application, environment and region limits blast radius. New vaults default to the **Azure RBAC** permission model. Tomasi creates separate vaults for the claims portal in test and production.
Recovery settings

**Soft delete** is always on and keeps deleted items for 7 to 90 days (90 by default), set at creation. **Purge protection** is optional but cannot be turned off once on, and stops anyone purging deleted items before the retention ends. Services using customer managed keys, such as Storage, require it.
Access flags and logging

Flags let VMs retrieve certificates, Azure Disk Encryption unwrap keys, and Resource Manager read secrets during template deployment. **Diagnostic settings** send AuditEvent logs of every data plane request to Log Analytics, and Event Grid can raise events when items near expiry.

check.q: Brightwater will use its own key to encrypt a storage account. What must be enabled on the vault that holds the key?
options: Public network access from all networks
check.why: Customer managed key scenarios require soft delete and purge protection so the key cannot be permanently destroyed early. Network and tier choices do not meet that requirement, and the template flag is for deployments.

lessons.key: Choose the Key Vault tier, one vault per app and environment, and turn on purge protection, which customer managed keys require.

lessons.title: Key Vault access and firewall
steps: Two planes

The **control plane** creates and configures vaults and uses Azure RBAC, such as Key Vault Contributor. The **data plane** reads secrets and uses keys, governed by the vault's permission model. **Key Vault Contributor never grants data access** by itself.
RBAC versus access policies

With **Azure RBAC** (recommended), data roles such as Key Vault Secrets User, Crypto User or Certificates Officer can be assigned at vault level or on one secret, and work with PIM. Legacy **access policies** apply to the whole vault, and anyone with Key Vault Contributor can edit them to grant themselves access.
Firewall options

Public access can be open, limited to **IP rules** (public addresses only) and **virtual network rules** using service endpoints, or disabled so only **private endpoints** work. A trusted Microsoft services bypass lets some Azure services through.
Gotchas

Firewall rules affect the data plane only, so management operations still work. The portal cannot list secrets unless the admin's IP is allowed. Tomasi disables public access to the production vault and uses a private endpoint with the privatelink vaultcore private DNS zone.

check.q: A Brightwater developer holds Key Vault Contributor and the vault uses access policies. Why is this a risk?
options: Contributor can read every secret directly
It can rewrite the policies to grant itself access
check.why: With access policies, Contributor can change the policies and give itself data rights. Contributor does not read secrets directly, which is the tempting answer, and purge protection applies to everyone.

lessons.key: Key Vault separates control and data planes, Azure RBAC is preferred over access policies, and private endpoints remove public access.

lessons.title: Managing keys, secrets and certificates
steps: Keys

Keys can be RSA or EC, software or HSM protected, and are used to encrypt, sign or **wrap** other keys. HSM key material never leaves the HSM, and you can bring your own key from an on premises HSM. Keys have activation and expiry dates.
Automatic rotation

A **rotation policy** creates a new key version after a set time or before expiry, and can notify through Event Grid first. Services using customer managed keys should point at the **versionless** key address so they pick up new versions automatically.
Secrets

Secrets hold passwords, connection strings and API keys, and each update creates a version. Expiry dates and Event Grid near expiry events let an Azure Function rotate a credential at its source and store the new value as a new version.
Certificates

A certificate in Key Vault also creates a key and a secret with the same name. Its **policy** sets subject, key type, validity and issuer, and **lifetime actions** auto renew or email contacts before expiry. Partnered CAs such as DigiCert and GlobalSign support auto renewal. Brightwater's portal TLS certificate now renews 30 days before expiry.

check.q: Brightwater's storage account uses a customer managed key, and Tomasi enables key rotation. How should the storage account reference the key so it uses each new version?
options: By the secret with the same name
By the exact current version ID
By copying the key into the storage account
check.why: A versionless reference lets the service pick up new versions as they are created. A fixed version would keep using the old key, and copying keys out of the vault defeats the purpose.

lessons.key: Rotate keys with a rotation policy and versionless references, rotate secrets with expiry events, and auto renew certificates with lifetime actions.

lessons.title: Secrets scanning and Defender for Key Vault
steps: Finding leaked secrets

Leaked SSH keys, connection strings and tokens let attackers move sideways. **Defender CSPM** scans for them agentlessly on VM disks, in cloud deployment resources and in connected Azure DevOps repositories. Machine secrets scanning also comes with Defender for Servers Plan 2.
Where findings appear

Findings show as recommendations, in asset inventory, in **cloud security explorer** queries and in **attack paths**, which show how a secret on an internet exposed VM could reach a critical asset. The fix is to rotate the credential, store it in Key Vault and have the workload read it with a managed identity.
Defender for Key Vault

**Microsoft Defender for Key Vault** watches vault operations and raises alerts for access from Tor or suspicious IPs, unusual users or apps, unusually high operation volumes, and patterns such as listing then reading many secrets, which suggests someone dumping the vault.
Responding

It is enabled per subscription in Defender for Cloud. For an alert, Tomasi identifies the source, contains it with the vault firewall or by removing the principal's access, measures impact from the AuditEvent logs, and rotates every affected secret, key and certificate.

check.q: Defender for Key Vault alerts that an app listed then read dozens of secrets it never normally touches. What should Tomasi do after containing the source?
options: Dismiss the alert because the app is known
Rotate every secret that was read
check.why: Any secret that may have been exposed must be rotated. Recognising the app does not mean it was not compromised, deleting the vault breaks production, and logs are needed to measure impact.

lessons.key: Defender CSPM finds leaked secrets on disks and in code, and Defender for Key Vault alerts on suspicious vault access that may need secrets rotated.

lessons.title: Azure Policy definitions and effects
steps: What a policy definition is

An **Azure Policy** definition is a JSON rule: if a resource matches conditions on its properties, then apply an **effect**. Thousands of built in definitions exist, and custom ones use property aliases when none fits. An **initiative** bundles definitions to assign together.
Effects that block or report

**Deny** blocks a non compliant create or update. **Audit** allows it but reports non compliance. **AuditIfNotExists** reports when a related resource, such as a diagnostic setting, is missing. **DenyAction** blocks specific actions such as delete.
Effects that change things

**Modify** adds or changes properties or tags on the request, and **deployIfNotExists** deploys a missing related resource using a template. Both need a managed identity with suitable roles. **Append** adds fields, **manual** records attestation by a person, and **disabled** turns a rule off.
At Brightwater

Tomasi assigns a deny policy so no storage account can allow anonymous blob access, a deployIfNotExists policy that adds diagnostic settings to every Key Vault, and a denyAction policy that stops anyone deleting the production SQL server.

check.q: Tomasi wants every new Key Vault to get a diagnostic setting automatically. Which effect does that?
check.why: DeployIfNotExists deploys a missing related resource such as a diagnostic setting, using a managed identity. Deny would block vault creation, audit only reports, and disabled does nothing.

lessons.key: Policy effects deny, audit, modify or deploy missing resources, and modify and deployIfNotExists need a managed identity.

lessons.title: Policy assignment, exemptions and remediation
steps: Assigning a policy

An **assignment** applies a definition or initiative at a scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource), inherited downwards. It can exclude child scopes, set parameters and include a managed identity for modify and deployIfNotExists. **Resource Policy Contributor** manages assignments.
Testing first

**Enforcement mode** can be set to do not enforce, so the policy is evaluated and reported without its effect being applied. Tomasi uses this to see how many storage accounts would fail before switching to deny.
Remediation tasks

Policies evaluate on create and update and in a regular compliance scan. Modify and deployIfNotExists act automatically only on new or changed resources, so existing non compliant resources are fixed with a **remediation task**.
Exemptions

An **exemption** marks a resource or scope as exempt, either as a **waiver** (non compliance accepted for now) or **mitigated** (the goal is met another way), with an optional expiry date. Brightwater exempts a legacy app's storage account for 60 days while it is migrated.

check.q: Brightwater assigns a deployIfNotExists policy, but 40 existing VMs remain non compliant. What should Tomasi run?
check.why: DeployIfNotExists only acts on new or updated resources automatically, so a remediation task fixes existing ones. Exempting them would hide the problem, and locks and new definitions do not deploy anything.

lessons.key: Assign policies at the right scope, test with do not enforce, fix existing resources with remediation tasks, and record waivers as exemptions.

lessons.title: Compliance, standards and recommendations in Defender for Cloud
steps: Regulatory compliance

**Regulatory compliance** in Defender for Cloud shows control by control how resources meet a standard. Each control maps to automatically checked recommendations: green passes, red fails, greyed out cannot be assessed automatically. The **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)** is on by default.
Adding standards

Standards such as ISO 27001, PCI DSS, NIST SP 800-53 and SOC 2 can be added once any paid Defender plan is on except Defender for Servers Plan 1 or Defender for APIs Plan 1, by someone with rights to assign policy. A passing dashboard is technical evidence, not certification.
Standards and recommendations

In Azure, each **security standard** is backed by a policy initiative. **Recommendations** have severity, risk level, affected resources and fix steps, often with quick fix or enforce buttons. Resources can be exempted, and **governance rules** assign owners and due dates.
Secure score and custom content

**Secure score** drops most for open high risk recommendations, and preview ones do not count. Custom recommendations can be written as KQL over the cloud security graph (needs Defender CSPM) or as custom Azure Policy definitions. Brightwater adds PCI DSS for its card payment component and assigns owners to every critical finding.

check.q: Brightwater wants PCI DSS tracked in Defender for Cloud, but the option is unavailable. Only Defender for Servers Plan 1 is enabled. What is needed?
options: Assign the standard with a resource lock
A qualifying paid plan, such as Defender CSPM
check.why: Adding regulatory standards needs a paid Defender plan other than Servers Plan 1 or APIs Plan 1. Foundational CSPM is free and not enough, and locks and Entra licences are unrelated.

lessons.key: Regulatory compliance maps standards to recommendations, extra standards need a qualifying paid plan, and recommendations feed secure score and governance.

lessons.title: Resource locks
steps: Two lock levels

**Resource locks** protect resources from accidental change. **CanNotDelete** allows reading and changing but not deleting. **ReadOnly** allows reading only. Locks can sit on a subscription, resource group or resource.
Locks beat roles

Locks override RBAC: even an Owner must remove the lock first. They are inherited by everything below, including resources created later, and the most restrictive applies. A lock on any resource also blocks deletion of its resource group.
Control plane only
Locks apply to management operations only. A lock on a storage account does not protect the blobs inside, and a ReadOnly lock on a SQL server does not stop data changes in its databases.
Side effects

Some operations are implemented as POST requests, so ReadOnly can break them: listing storage keys fails, VMs in a ReadOnly group cannot start, and App Service plans cannot scale. Only roles with lock permissions, such as Owner and User Access Administrator, manage locks, and Contributor cannot. Brightwater puts CanNotDelete on its production resource groups.

check.q: Tomasi puts a ReadOnly lock on the resource group holding Brightwater's batch VMs, and the nightly job can no longer start them. Why?
options: The lock stops the VMs' scheduled tasks
ReadOnly removes the VMs' managed identities
Locks block all outbound network traffic
check.why: Starting a VM is a management operation that ReadOnly blocks. CanNotDelete would have prevented deletion while letting the job run. Locks do not touch identities, scheduled tasks or networking.

lessons.key: CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks override RBAC, are inherited, protect only management operations, and ReadOnly can break routine actions.

lessons.title: Built-in and custom role assignments
steps: Who, what, where

**Azure RBAC** answers who can do what where. Prefer **groups** over individuals and managed identities for workloads, choose the narrowest **job function role** (such as Virtual Machine Contributor or Storage Blob Data Reader) and assign at the lowest scope, because permissions inherit downwards.
Privileged roles

**Owner**, **Contributor**, **User Access Administrator** and **Role Based Access Control Administrator** are high risk. Contributor manages resources but cannot assign roles. RBAC Administrator only manages role assignments and supports **conditions** that limit which roles it may assign. Owner of a storage account does not automatically read data: data roles grant data actions.
Custom Azure roles

A custom Azure role lists Actions, NotActions, DataActions and NotDataActions with assignable scopes. NotActions is not a deny: another assignment can still grant the action. Roles with data actions cannot be assigned at management group scope. A good start is cloning a built in role and trimming it.
Custom Entra roles

Custom **Entra roles** are built from directory permissions, need P1 for assignees, and can be scoped to the tenant, an administrative unit or a single app. Azure roles never grant directory permissions, and Entra roles never grant Azure resource rights.

check.q: A Brightwater custom Azure role lists delete in NotActions, but the user can still delete resources. Why?
options: Custom roles take effect only after a day
Delete is a data action, not an action
NotActions applies only at management group scope
check.why: NotActions only subtracts from that role's own actions. If another assignment, such as Contributor, grants delete, the union of assignments allows it. Real denial needs a lock or a deny assignment.

lessons.key: Assign narrow job roles to groups at low scope, treat Owner and User Access Administrator as high risk, and remember NotActions is not a deny.

lessons.title: Finding and fixing overprivileged access
steps: Least privilege
**Least privilege** means the smallest role, at the lowest scope, for the shortest time. Azure RBAC is additive, so a principal's effective rights are the union of every assignment.
Finding the problems

Tomasi lists role assignments in access control and with Azure Resource Graph to find Owners at subscription or management group scope. Defender for Cloud recommends limiting subscription owners and removing blocked or guest accounts with owner rights. **CIEM** in Defender CSPM finds inactive and overprovisioned identities across Azure, AWS and GCP based on actual use.
Fixing them

Replace Owner and Contributor with job specific roles, move assignments down to resource groups or resources, assign to groups, and convert standing privileged assignments to **PIM eligible** with approval. Remove orphaned assignments shown as identity not found, and unused service principals.
Keeping it fixed

Recurring **access reviews** of Azure roles through PIM, with auto apply removing denied access, stop the problem coming back. RBAC conditions limit what delegated admins can assign. Brightwater cuts its subscription Owners from eleven to three.

check.q: CIEM shows a Brightwater service principal holds Contributor on the subscription but has only ever read one storage container. What is the best fix?
options: Move it to Contributor on one resource group
Storage Blob Data Reader on that container
Leave it, as it has never misused the role
Make it eligible for Contributor in PIM
check.why: Least privilege means matching the role and scope to real use, which is read access to one container. Contributor on a resource group is still far too broad, and PIM eligibility helps people rather than an always running service principal.

lessons.key: Find broad and unused rights with role listings, Defender recommendations and CIEM, then narrow roles and scopes, use PIM and review access regularly.

lessons.title: Azure Backup security features
steps: Attackers go after backups
Ransomware crews often delete backups before encrypting production. Recovery Services vaults and Backup vaults offer layers to stop that.
Soft delete and immutability

**Enhanced soft delete** keeps deleted backup data recoverable for 14 to 180 days, and always on soft delete cannot be disabled. An **immutable vault** blocks deleting recovery points before expiry or reducing retention. It can be enabled and later **locked**, after which it cannot be undone.
Multi user authorisation

**Multi user authorisation (MUA)** uses a separate **Resource Guard** owned by a security admin, ideally in another subscription or tenant. Critical operations, such as disabling soft delete or reducing protection, need a permission on the Resource Guard, which the security admin grants only temporarily, ideally through PIM.
Other controls

Backup roles (Backup Contributor, Operator, Reader), customer managed key encryption, private endpoints and alerts in Azure Monitor and Defender for Cloud complete the picture. Brightwater locks immutability on the claims database vault and puts its Resource Guard in a separate security subscription.

check.q: Tomasi wants a backup admin to be unable to disable soft delete on Brightwater's vault without a second person approving. What should he configure?
options: A CanNotDelete lock on the vault
Multi user authorisation with a Resource Guard
Increase the soft delete period to 180 days
Immutable vault in the enabled state only
check.why: MUA requires permission on a Resource Guard controlled by someone else before critical operations such as disabling soft delete. A lock does not cover backup settings, and a longer period or reversible immutability does not stop the change itself.

lessons.key: Protect backups with enhanced soft delete, immutable vaults and multi user authorisation through a separately owned Resource Guard.

lessons.title: Security controls with infrastructure as code
steps: No secrets in templates

**Infrastructure as code (IaC)** describes resources in files such as Bicep or ARM templates. Secrets never belong in them: use secure parameters and reference Key Vault secrets, with getSecret in Bicep or a Key Vault reference in a parameter file. The vault needs template deployment enabled.
Deploying controls as code

Locks, role assignments, policy assignments, diagnostic settings and private endpoints can all be declared in templates, so every environment gets the same controls. **Policy as code** keeps definitions and assignments in Git, deployed through pipelines.
Deployment stacks

**Deployment stacks** manage a set of resources as one unit with **deny settings** that block deletes, or writes and deletes, on the managed resources, with a few excluded principals such as the pipeline identity.
Scanning before deployment

**Microsoft Security DevOps** runs scanners such as Template Analyzer, Checkov and Terrascan in GitHub or Azure DevOps pipelines, and results appear in Defender for Cloud DevOps security. what-if deployments preview changes. Brightwater's pipeline now fails if a template opens storage to anonymous access.

check.q: Brightwater's Bicep template needs the SQL admin password during deployment. How should Tomasi provide it?
options: Email it to the pipeline owner
Hard code it in the template
Put it in a plain text parameter file in Git
Reference a Key Vault secret with getSecret
check.why: Referencing a Key Vault secret keeps the password out of code and history. Hard coding it or storing it in Git exposes it to anyone with repository access.

lessons.key: Keep secrets out of templates with Key Vault references, deploy controls as code, protect with deployment stacks and scan templates in the pipeline.

modules.title: Secure storage, databases and networking
modules.intro: Data is what attackers want, and networks decide how they reach it. This module secures storage accounts, Azure SQL and other databases, and the network paths between them (about 25 to 30 percent of the exam). Brightwater Insurance keeps claim photos in Storage, policies in Azure SQL, and connects branch offices and remote assessors to Azure, so every lesson has a real target.

lessons.title: Storage account baseline and encryption
steps: The account baseline

Before anything else, Tomasi locks down the account. **Secure transfer required** rejects plain HTTP. **Minimum TLS version** should be 1.2. **Allow blob anonymous access** set to false means no container can be read anonymously, whatever its own setting. **Public network access** can be open, limited to chosen networks, or disabled.
Policy keeps it that way
Built in Azure Policy definitions, such as requiring secure transfer or disallowing anonymous access, stop new accounts drifting from the baseline.
Customer managed keys

Storage always encrypts data. With **customer managed keys**, the account wraps its data keys with a key in Key Vault or Managed HSM. The vault needs soft delete and purge protection, and the account's managed identity needs get, wrap and unwrap rights. Disabling the key cuts off access to the data.
Infrastructure encryption

**Infrastructure encryption** adds a second encryption layer with a separate Microsoft managed key. It must be chosen when the account is created and cannot be changed later. **Encryption scopes** allow different keys per container. Brightwater uses its own key for the claim photos account.

check.q: Brightwater's compliance team wants double encryption on a new claims archive account. When must Tomasi choose infrastructure encryption?
options: Any time from the encryption page
Only after enabling customer managed keys
check.why: Infrastructure encryption can only be set at creation and cannot be turned on or off later. It does not depend on customer managed keys.

lessons.key: Secure storage with HTTPS, TLS 1.2, no anonymous access and limited network access, and use customer managed keys or infrastructure encryption where needed.

lessons.title: Azure Storage firewall rules
steps: Default deny

Choosing **enabled from selected networks** makes the storage firewall deny by default. Only listed sources reach the public endpoint, and they still need valid authorisation. The firewall never grants data access by itself.
IP and network rules

**IP rules** allow public IPv4 addresses or ranges only, not private ranges, and do not apply to clients in the same Azure region. **Virtual network rules** allow a subnet that has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint, so traffic arrives from that subnet.
Resource instances and trusted services

**Resource instance rules** allow a specific instance of a supported service in the same tenant, such as one analytics workspace. **Trusted service exceptions** let certain Azure services, such as logging and backup, connect with strong authentication.
At Brightwater

The claims photo account allows only the portal's subnet and Brightwater's office public IP, plus trusted services for backup. A SAS restricted to an IP can never grant more than the network rules allow.

check.q: Tomasi adds an IP rule for an Azure VM in the same region as the storage account, but the VM is still blocked. Why?
options: The VM needs a SAS as well as the rule
IP rules apply only to IPv6 clients
Same region clients ignore IP rules
The rule needs a priority number
check.why: Same region traffic uses private Azure addresses, so IP rules have no effect. A virtual network rule with a service endpoint, or a private endpoint, fixes it. IP rules are IPv4 and have no priorities.

lessons.key: The storage firewall denies by default once enabled, allowing listed public IPs, subnets with service endpoints, resource instances and trusted services.

lessons.title: Defender for Storage
steps: What it watches

**Microsoft Defender for Storage** raises alerts for suspicious activity such as access from Tor or known malicious IPs, unusual data extraction and anomalous SAS use. It needs no resource logs and does not affect performance.
Malware scanning

**Malware scanning** checks blobs with Microsoft Defender Antivirus either **on upload** (every new or changed blob) or **on demand** (an account, container or single blob, for example during an incident). A monthly cap per account, 10,000 GB by default, stops scanning when reached. It is billed per GB scanned.
Results and response

Results are written as **blob index tags**, security alerts, Event Grid events and a Log Analytics table. Tags are not tamper proof. Responses include the built in option to soft delete malicious blobs, access conditions that block unscanned or malicious blobs, or an Azure Function that moves clean files onward.
Sensitive data and enablement

**Sensitive data threat detection** raises the severity of alerts that touch data classified as sensitive. Microsoft recommends enabling the plan at subscription level, with per account overrides. Brightwater scans every claim photo upload, because customers upload files directly.

check.q: Brightwater customers upload claim photos and documents directly to Storage. Tomasi wants every upload checked for malware automatically. Which setting fits?
options: On-demand malware scanning once a month
check.why: On-upload scanning checks every new or modified blob as it arrives. Monthly on-demand scans leave a gap, and encryption and locks do not detect malware.

lessons.key: Defender for Storage detects suspicious access and scans uploads for malware, with results as tags, alerts and events for automated response.

lessons.title: Managing access to storage
steps: SAS types

A **shared access signature (SAS)** grants limited, time bound access. A **user delegation SAS** is signed with Entra credentials, lasts at most seven days and is the recommended type. A **service SAS** and an **account SAS** are signed with an account key.
Stored access policies

A **stored access policy** on a container sets start, expiry and permissions for any service SAS that references it, and up to five can exist per container. Deleting or changing the policy revokes those SAS tokens. Without one, a key signed SAS can only be revoked by regenerating the key. An **expiry policy** can cap SAS lifetimes.
Entra ID data roles

Data access through Entra uses **data roles** such as Storage Blob Data Reader, Contributor and Owner, assigned at the narrowest scope. Plain Reader cannot read blob data. Control plane roles that can list keys effectively get full data access through those keys.
Turning off Shared Key

Anyone with an account key has full access. Tomasi assigns the policy that audits shared key access, finds remaining key and SAS clients in metrics and logs, moves them to Entra ID, sets **allow shared key access** to false, then switches the policy to deny.

check.q: A partner's service SAS for a Brightwater container leaked. It references a stored access policy. What is the fastest way to revoke it?
options: Wait for the SAS to expire
Delete or change the stored access policy
check.why: A SAS tied to a stored access policy is revoked by deleting or changing the policy, without disrupting other key users. Rotating keys also works but breaks everything signed with that key, waiting leaves the leak open, and Entra roles do not govern a SAS.

lessons.key: Prefer user delegation SAS and Entra data roles, use stored access policies for revocable service SAS, and disable Shared Key access when you can.

lessons.title: Azure SQL platform security
steps: Network access

Azure SQL can disable public access (private endpoints only) or allow selected networks. **Server level IP rules** cover every database, **database level rules** cover one. The option to allow Azure services admits all of Azure, including other customers, so explicit rules or private access are better. Minimum TLS should be 1.2.
Entra only authentication

**Microsoft Entra only authentication** lets only Entra identities connect, so SQL logins stop working. An Entra admin must be set first. Owner, Contributor or **SQL Security Manager** can switch it on, while SQL Server Contributor cannot, which keeps duties separate.
Transparent data encryption

**TDE** encrypts data at rest with a database key protected by a **TDE protector**: service managed by default, or a customer managed key in Key Vault. If access to that key is removed, the database becomes inaccessible. TDE does not hide data from anyone who can query it.
Always Encrypted

**Always Encrypted** encrypts chosen columns in the client driver, so the server only stores ciphertext. A column master key in a trusted store protects the column encryption key. **Deterministic** encryption allows equality lookups, while **randomised** is stronger. Brightwater encrypts policyholders' bank numbers so even database admins cannot read them.

check.q: Brightwater wants database administrators unable to read policyholders' bank account numbers, while the app still uses them. Which feature fits?
options: TDE with a service managed key
check.why: Always Encrypted keeps the column encrypted on the server, so admins see ciphertext unless they hold the column master key. TDE only protects data at rest and shows plaintext to anyone who can query it.

lessons.key: Lock down SQL network access, enforce Entra only authentication, use TDE for data at rest, and Always Encrypted to hide columns from admins.

lessons.title: Auditing Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance
steps: SQL Database auditing

**Auditing** records database events for compliance and investigations. By default it captures completed queries and successful and failed logins. A **server level** policy covers every database on the server, and a database level policy runs alongside it, producing two records if both are on.
Destinations

Audit logs can go to **storage** (files readable in SSMS), **Log Analytics** or **Event Hubs**. Storage should be reached with a managed identity, and a storage firewall needs trusted services allowed. Deleting the diagnostic setting silently stops Log Analytics auditing, so Tomasi alerts on its removal.
Managed Instance auditing

**SQL Managed Instance** is configured like SQL Server with T-SQL: a credential for the storage container, a server audit to that URL (or to an external monitor for Log Analytics), an audit specification listing groups such as failed logins, then turning the audit on.
Microsoft support operations

Both services can audit operations performed by Microsoft support engineers. On Managed Instance this is a separate audit. Brightwater sends all SQL audit logs to Log Analytics and keeps a copy in immutable storage.

check.q: Tomasi wants auditing on every existing and future database on Brightwater's SQL logical server. Where should he enable it?
check.why: A server level audit policy applies to all existing and new databases on that server. Database level policies must be set one by one and run in addition to any server audit.

lessons.key: Enable server level auditing for all databases, send logs to storage, Log Analytics or Event Hubs, and configure Managed Instance auditing with T-SQL.

lessons.title: Defender for Databases
steps: One plan, four parts

**Defender for Databases** covers **Azure SQL** (databases, managed instances and Synapse dedicated pools), **SQL Server on machines** (Azure VMs, on premises and other clouds through Arc), **open source relational databases** (PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible servers and some Amazon RDS engines) and **Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL**.
Vulnerability assessment

**SQL vulnerability assessment** scans for misconfigurations, excessive permissions and unprotected sensitive data, and lets you approve a **baseline** so accepted results stop being flagged. Express configuration, recommended and at no extra cost, stores results for you.
Threat protection

Threat protection raises alerts such as **potential SQL injection**, brute force sign in attempts, access from unusual locations or suspicious IPs, and, for Cosmos DB, suspicious key enumeration and data extraction. Alerts carry MITRE tactics and flow to Defender XDR and Sentinel.
Turning it on

In Defender for Cloud environment settings, switching **Databases** on enables all parts for the subscription, or parts can be chosen individually. Brightwater enables it at subscription level so new databases are covered automatically.

check.q: Brightwater runs a SQL Server instance on an on premises VM that is connected with Azure Arc. Which part of Defender for Databases protects it?
options: Defender for SQL Servers on Machines
check.why: SQL Server on VMs, on premises or in other clouds through Arc, is covered by Defender for SQL Servers on Machines. The Azure SQL part covers PaaS, the open source part covers PostgreSQL and MySQL, and Servers Plan 1 does not include SQL threat protection.

lessons.key: Defender for Databases covers Azure SQL, SQL on machines, open source databases and Cosmos DB with vulnerability assessment and threat alerts.

lessons.title: Network security groups and application security groups
steps: NSG rules

A **network security group (NSG)** rule has a priority, source and destination (address, range, service tag or ASG), ports, protocol and allow or deny. Processing stops at the first match. NSGs are stateful, so replies to allowed traffic return automatically. Default rules allow traffic inside the virtual network and deny other inbound traffic.
Subnet and network card

Inbound traffic is checked by the subnet NSG first, then the network card NSG, and outbound the other way round. Traffic must be allowed by both. **Service tags** stand for Microsoft maintained address lists, so rules do not break when Azure addresses change.
Application security groups

An **application security group (ASG)** groups VMs by role, such as web or database, so a rule can say allow web to database on port 1433. As the app scales, network cards are added to the group with no address lists to update. All members must be in the same virtual network.
Flow logs

NSG flow logs are being retired in favour of **virtual network flow logs** with Traffic analytics. Brightwater's claims app uses three ASGs, and its database subnet only accepts traffic from the app tier ASG.

check.q: Brightwater's web tier scales from 4 to 20 VMs during storms. Tomasi wants NSG rules that never need IP address updates. What should he use?
options: A rule per VM IP address
Service tags for the web subnet
check.why: ASGs let rules target roles rather than addresses, so new VMs simply join the group. Per IP and augmented rules need edits as the tier scales, and service tags describe Microsoft services, not your VMs.

lessons.key: NSGs filter traffic by first matching rule at subnet and NIC level, and ASGs let rules target application roles instead of addresses.

lessons.title: Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules
steps: Central rules across many networks

**Azure Virtual Network Manager (AVNM)** manages many virtual networks from one place. Its scope covers management groups or subscriptions. **Network groups** collect virtual networks, either statically or dynamically by conditions such as a tag.
Security admin rules

A **security admin configuration** holds rule collections targeted at network groups. Nothing applies until the configuration is **deployed** to regions, and only one security admin configuration can be deployed per region.
Three actions

**Deny** blocks traffic before NSGs ever see it. **Always allow** permits traffic that NSGs cannot block. **Allow** permits it at the admin layer and then NSG rules still decide. Lower priority numbers win.
Why it matters

App teams own their NSGs, but some rules must never be overridden. Tomasi deploys a deny rule for inbound RDP and SSH from the internet to every Brightwater virtual network, and an always allow rule for the vulnerability scanner.

check.q: Tomasi needs a rule blocking inbound RDP from the internet that application teams cannot override with their own NSGs. Which tool and action fit?
options: An NSG rule at priority 100 in each subnet
A route table sending RDP to a firewall
An AVNM security admin rule set to Allow
An AVNM security admin rule with Deny
check.why: AVNM deny rules are evaluated before NSGs, so app teams cannot override them. Teams can edit their own NSGs, an AVNM Allow defers to NSGs, and routing alone does not stop the traffic.

lessons.key: AVNM security admin rules apply centrally to groups of virtual networks, with Deny and Always allow taking precedence over NSGs.

lessons.title: Securing Azure Virtual WAN
steps: Virtual WAN

**Azure Virtual WAN** provides managed hubs connecting virtual networks, branches and remote users. Only the **Standard** type supports Azure Firewall and other security appliances, so Brightwater upgrades from Basic.
Secured hubs
A **secured hub** is a Virtual WAN hub with Azure Firewall deployed through **Azure Firewall Manager** using a firewall policy, or with a supported partner appliance or service.
Routing intent

**Routing intent** decides what the hub's firewall inspects. An **internet traffic** policy sends internet bound traffic from spokes, branches and users through it. A **private traffic** policy sends branch to network, network to network and hub to hub traffic through it. For hub to hub inspection, every hub needs routing intent.
Partners

Security partner providers can filter internet traffic while Azure Firewall handles private traffic. Brightwater sets both routing intent policies on its Auckland and Sydney hubs so branch traffic to Azure is inspected.

check.q: Brightwater wants all branch to Azure traffic through its Virtual WAN hub inspected by Azure Firewall. What should Tomasi configure?
options: Upgrade to Standard but skip routing intent
Routing intent with a private traffic policy
An internet traffic routing policy only
An NSG on each branch connection
check.why: A private traffic policy sends branch to network traffic through the hub firewall. Standard without routing intent does not force inspection, an internet policy covers internet bound traffic only, and NSGs do not route traffic through a firewall.

lessons.key: Secure Virtual WAN with Standard secured hubs and routing intent policies that send internet and private traffic through the firewall.

lessons.title: Securing VPN connections
steps: Site to site VPN

A **site to site** connection links an Azure virtual network gateway to a local network gateway that represents the on premises device. New gateways use zone redundant SKUs. The Basic SKU is for testing and lacks features such as custom IPsec policies.
Custom IPsec and IKE policy

A **custom IPsec/IKE policy** sets the exact encryption, integrity, Diffie Hellman group and lifetime for a connection, and must match the on premises device. A strong example uses AES 256 and GCM algorithms with high DH groups. A strong pre shared key should be rotated.
Point to site VPN

**Point to site** VPN connects individual devices. **OpenVPN** works through most firewalls on port 443 and supports every major platform. Authentication can be certificates, RADIUS or **Microsoft Entra ID**, which needs OpenVPN and the Azure VPN Client.
Conditional Access for VPN

With Entra ID authentication, **Conditional Access** applies to the VPN sign in, so Brightwater can require MFA and a compliant device before a loss assessor's laptop joins the network. Certificate based clients are revoked by adding them to a revocation list.

check.q: Brightwater wants remote assessors' VPN sign in to require MFA and a compliant device. Which point to site set up fits?
check.why: Entra ID authentication, which uses OpenVPN and the Azure VPN Client, lets Conditional Access require MFA and device compliance. Certificate and RADIUS options authenticate without Conditional Access.

lessons.key: Use custom IPsec/IKE policies for strong site to site tunnels, and OpenVPN with Entra ID authentication so Conditional Access protects point to site VPN.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra Private Access
steps: Identity aware access instead of VPN
**Microsoft Entra Private Access** gives users access to specific private apps over TCP and UDP based on identity, rather than opening a whole network through a VPN.
Components

Devices run the **Global Secure Access client** with the Private Access forwarding profile on. A **private network connector**, a light Windows Server agent near the apps, makes only outbound connections, so no inbound firewall ports are needed. Connectors sit in groups, and more than one per group gives failover.
Quick Access and per app

**Quick Access** puts a broad set of internal addresses into one app as a fast VPN replacement. **Per app** applications each have their own segments, assignments and Conditional Access, and take priority over overlapping Quick Access segments. Private DNS lets users reach internal short names.
Set up and licensing

The order is connector group, apps and segments, user assignments (no nested groups), Conditional Access, then turning on the forwarding profile. It needs a Private Access or Entra Suite licence. Brightwater publishes its on premises claims archive as a per app application requiring a compliant device.

check.q: Brightwater's security team refuses to open any inbound firewall ports for remote access to the claims archive. Why does Private Access satisfy them?
options: It tunnels over a site to site VPN
It publishes the server on a public IP
It routes through Azure Firewall DNAT
check.why: Private network connectors reach out to Microsoft's service, so no inbound ports are needed. Site to site VPN, public IPs and DNAT all involve inbound paths.

lessons.key: Private Access uses outbound only connectors and per app applications with Conditional Access to replace broad VPN access.

lessons.title: Private endpoints and DNS
steps: What a private endpoint does

A **private endpoint** gives a specific PaaS resource, such as one storage account's blob service, a private IP address in your subnet. Traffic stays on Microsoft's network and works from peered networks and on premises. Once endpoints exist, Tomasi sets the resource's public network access to disabled.
Sub resources and approval

Each endpoint targets a sub resource, such as blob, file, sqlServer or vault. Approval is automatic if you have rights on the target, otherwise the owner approves a manual request. A **service endpoint**, by contrast, keeps the public address but lets the service firewall recognise your subnet, and does not work from on premises.
DNS makes it work

Azure points the normal name, such as the account's blob address, at a privatelink name. A **private DNS zone**, such as the privatelink blob zone, linked to your networks resolves that name to the private IP. A **DNS zone group** on the endpoint creates and removes records automatically.
On premises and policies

On premises clients need DNS forwarding to a resolver in Azure. Apps keep using the normal name, never the privatelink name. NSGs and route tables only apply to private endpoints when network policies are enabled on the subnet.

check.q: Brightwater created a private endpoint for its storage account, but VMs still resolve the account to a public IP. What is most likely missing?
options: A service endpoint on the subnet
check.why: Without the privatelink DNS zone linked to the network, the name still resolves to the public IP. A service endpoint is a different mechanism, an unapproved endpoint would not change DNS, and network policies govern NSGs and routes.

lessons.key: Private endpoints give PaaS resources private IPs, and private DNS zones linked to your networks make the normal names resolve to them.

lessons.title: Azure Private Link service
steps: Publishing, not consuming

A private endpoint consumes a service privately. A **Private Link service** lets you **publish** your own service so other virtual networks, tenants or customers can reach it through their own private endpoints.
Provider set up

The app sits behind a **Standard Load Balancer**, and the Private Link service is created on its frontend. Consumer traffic is source translated to NAT addresses from a chosen subnet. **TCP Proxy v2** passes the original client details if the app needs them.
Controlling who connects

**Visibility** limits who can find the service: RBAC only, chosen subscriptions or anyone with the alias. **Auto approval** lists subscriptions approved automatically, and others wait for manual approval. Consumers use a globally unique **alias** instead of your resource ID.
At Brightwater

Brightwater publishes its claims status API to three partner repair networks through a Private Link service, visible only to their subscriptions. Each partner creates a private endpoint, which stays pending until Tomasi approves it.

check.q: Brightwater wants partner companies to reach its internal claims API privately from their own Azure networks. What should Tomasi create?
options: A public endpoint with WAF and IP rules
A private endpoint to the partner's network
check.why: A Private Link service publishes your service so consumers connect through their own private endpoints. A public endpoint exposes it to the internet, a private endpoint consumes rather than publishes, and peering connects whole networks rather than one service.

lessons.key: Private Link service publishes your own service behind a Standard Load Balancer to consumers' private endpoints, controlled by visibility and approval.

lessons.title: Azure Firewall
steps: SKUs

**Azure Firewall** Basic suits small sites with alert only threat intelligence. **Standard** adds threat intelligence deny, DNS proxy and web categories. **Premium** adds **TLS inspection**, signature based **IDPS** and full URL filtering.
Firewall policy

Rules live in a **firewall policy** managed in Azure Firewall Manager, organised into rule collection groups holding **DNAT**, **network** and **application** collections. Threat intelligence is checked first, then DNAT, network and application rules. First match wins and unmatched traffic is denied. A parent policy's rules take precedence over a child's.
Routing traffic to it

Spoke networks send traffic to the firewall with user defined routes in hub and spoke designs, or routing intent in Virtual WAN. Inbound web apps should use a web application firewall instead of DNAT.
Premium features

**TLS inspection** decrypts outbound and east west traffic using an intermediate CA certificate stored in Key Vault, read through a user assigned managed identity. Without it, IDPS only sees unencrypted traffic. Brightwater uses Premium to inspect traffic between its claims app and payment services.

check.q: Brightwater's firewall must detect attacks hidden inside encrypted outbound HTTPS traffic. What does Tomasi need?
options: Azure Firewall Standard with web categories
Azure Firewall Basic with threat intelligence
Application Gateway WAF in prevention mode
Azure Firewall Premium with TLS inspection
check.why: Only Premium can decrypt outbound TLS so IDPS and URL filtering see inside. Standard and Basic cannot inspect encrypted content, and Application Gateway WAF protects inbound web apps rather than outbound traffic.

lessons.key: Azure Firewall policies process threat intelligence, DNAT, network then application rules, and Premium adds TLS inspection and IDPS.

lessons.title: Evaluating rules with Network Watcher
steps: Effective security rules

**Network Watcher** diagnoses network problems. **Effective security rules** shows, for one network card, the combined rules from the subnet NSG, the card's NSG and AVNM security admin rules, with service tags expanded. It shows what actually applies.
IP flow verify and NSG diagnostics

**IP flow verify** takes a VM, direction, protocol and addresses and returns allowed or denied with the name of the rule that decided. **NSG diagnostics** does similar checks for more resource types and can suggest a rule to fix the problem.
Routing checks

**Next hop** shows where traffic from a VM goes next, such as a virtual appliance, the internet or nothing, revealing routes that bypass the firewall. **Connection troubleshoot** tests a connection end to end.
A typical investigation

When the claims app cannot reach its database, Tomasi runs IP flow verify to find the blocking rule, effective security rules to see which NSG it comes from, and next hop to confirm traffic is routed through the firewall. **VNet flow logs** with Traffic analytics show real flows over time.

check.q: A Brightwater VM cannot connect to a database on port 1433. Tomasi wants to know exactly which rule blocks it. Which tool should he run first?
check.why: IP flow verify reports whether the traffic is allowed and names the deciding rule. Next hop shows routing rather than rule decisions, and traffic analytics and packet capture are slower and less direct.

lessons.key: Network Watcher's effective security rules, IP flow verify and next hop pinpoint which rule blocks traffic and where it is routed.

modules.title: Secure compute
modules.intro: Compute is where code runs: AI apps and agents, virtual machines, containers and app platforms (about 20 to 25 percent of the exam). Brightwater Insurance is rolling out Microsoft 365 Copilot, a Copilot Studio agent for staff, and a Foundry claims assistant for customers, alongside VMs, AKS, Functions and App Service. This module secures each of them, starting with AI.

lessons.title: Finding and containing overshared SharePoint content
steps: Why oversharing matters for AI

Microsoft 365 Copilot does not add permissions: it can read whatever each user can already read. If a site is shared with everyone in the company, Copilot can surface its contents to anyone who asks the right question. Fixing oversharing is the first step before rolling out Copilot.
Finding exposure

**SharePoint Advanced Management** includes **data access governance reports**: sharing link activity, content shared with everyone except external users, a sensitivity label snapshot across sites, permission state reports, and every site a given user can reach.
Containing it

A **site access review** asks site owners to confirm or remove access. **Restricted access control** limits a site to members of chosen groups, even if items inside are shared more widely. **Restricted Content Discovery** hides a site's content from organisation wide search and from Copilot, while people with access can still open files directly.
Choosing the control

Restricted Content Discovery changes discoverability, while restricted access control changes who can get in. Neither replaces fixing permissions. Brightwater finds its HR investigations site shared with everyone, so Tomasi applies Restricted Content Discovery at once and sends the owners an access review.

check.q: Brightwater wants an overshared site hidden from Copilot answers straight away, while its owners clean up permissions. Which control fits?
check.why: Restricted Content Discovery removes the site from organisation search and Copilot quickly. A report only shows the problem, and storage firewalls and locks do not affect SharePoint discovery.

lessons.key: Copilot follows existing permissions, so find oversharing with data access governance reports and contain it with Restricted Content Discovery or restricted access control.

lessons.title: Data Security Posture Management for AI
steps: What DSPM for AI does
**Data Security Posture Management (DSPM)** for AI in Microsoft Purview shows how people use Copilot, enterprise AI apps and third party AI sites, and where sensitive data is at risk.
Reports and activity

Reports and **activity explorer** group AI interactions by Copilot experiences and agents, enterprise AI apps and other AI apps, with events such as AI interactions, sensitive information found and visits to AI websites.
One click policies and assessments

Recommended **one click policies** turn on data loss prevention, insider risk and communication compliance policies for AI, collecting data within about a day. **Data risk assessments** find oversharing in SharePoint: a default weekly assessment of the top 100 sites, plus custom ones that expire after 30 days.
Prerequisites

Purview **Audit** must be on. Seeing third party AI sites also needs devices onboarded to Purview and the Purview browser extension. Tomasi learns that claims staff paste policy numbers into a public chatbot, and turns on the recommended DLP policy to block it.

check.q: Tomasi wants to see whether Brightwater staff paste sensitive data into third party AI websites. What must be in place besides Purview Audit?
options: Defender for Cloud Apps discovery alone
Device onboarding and the browser extension
check.why: Third party AI site activity is captured from onboarded devices through the Purview browser extension. Data risk assessments look at SharePoint oversharing, communication compliance covers messages, and discovery alone does not capture what users type into AI sites.

lessons.key: DSPM for AI reports AI usage and sensitive data risk, offers one click protective policies, and needs Audit plus device onboarding for third party AI sites.

lessons.title: Real-time protection for Copilot Studio agents
steps: Checking actions before they run

A Copilot Studio agent builds a plan of tools to call for each prompt. **Real time protection during agent runtime** sends that plan and its inputs to Microsoft Defender before each tool runs, and Defender answers allow or block.
Setting it up

In the Defender portal, security for AI agents, Tomasi turns on agent protection and real time protection and copies the Defender address. A Power Platform admin enables Defender threat protection for Copilot Studio agents, pastes the address and creates an Entra app, then gives the app ID back to Tomasi to finish the connection.
Behaviour to know

Defender must answer within about one second. If it does not, the agent **fails open** and the tool runs. Protection applies to new sessions only. Blocked calls appear as alerts in incidents and alerts.
Supporting data

The Microsoft 365 app connector in Defender for Cloud Apps must be connected so audit data and alerts flow in. Brightwater's staff agent can look up and update claim records, so stopping a manipulated plan before it acts matters.

check.q: If Defender does not respond within about a second during a Copilot Studio tool check, what happens?
options: The agent blocks every tool permanently
The agent fails open and runs the tool
check.why: Microsoft documents that the agent fails open if the check times out, so the tool runs. That is why other controls such as least privilege for agent tools still matter.

lessons.key: Real time protection checks each Copilot Studio tool call with Defender before it runs, fails open on timeout, and applies to new sessions.

lessons.title: Conditional Access and access for Entra Agent ID
steps: Agents have identities

**Microsoft Entra Agent ID** gives AI agents their own identities. An agent can act **on behalf of a user** (user policies apply), **as itself** with an **agent identity**, or as an **agent user** account. Each path needs its own Conditional Access thinking.
Conditional Access for agent identities

Policies can target all agent identities, chosen ones, agents with custom security attributes, or an **agent identity blueprint** covering all agents built from it. The only grant control is **block**, because agents cannot do MFA, and the only condition is **agent risk** from ID Protection. Policies for all users do not cover agent users.
Owners, sponsors and managers

An **owner** is the technical admin who can change the agent's settings and credentials. A **sponsor**, required for agent identities, is the business person accountable for it and decides on renewal. A **manager** places it in the organisation. If a sponsor leaves, sponsorship passes to their manager.
Governing access

**Access packages** in ID Governance can grant agents group memberships, API permissions and roles, with expiry and sponsor driven extension. The **Agent ID Administrator** role manages agents tenant wide. Tomasi blocks any Brightwater agent identity rated high risk.

check.q: Tomasi creates a Conditional Access policy for Brightwater's agent identities. Which grant control can he use?
check.why: Agent identities cannot complete interactive steps such as MFA, so block is the only grant control. Device and terms of use controls apply to agent user accounts, not agent identities acting as themselves.

lessons.key: Entra Agent ID policies can only block, using agent risk as a condition, and every agent identity needs an accountable sponsor.

lessons.title: Agent blast radius and management
steps: Measuring blast radius

An agent's **blast radius** comes from three things: its **permissions** (tenant wide application permissions reach far more than delegated or selected ones), its **knowledge sources** and their sensitivity, and its **capabilities**, especially actions that send data out, such as emailing or running code.
In Defender XDR

The Defender portal's **AI agents** inventory gives Foundry and some other cloud agents a risk score, recommendations and attack paths on a map. Prebuilt advanced hunting queries and the AIAgentsInfo table show each agent's tools, knowledge and authentication, while CloudAppEvents shows what it did.
Shrinking it

Rank attack paths by how critical the target is, not just their length. Replace broad scopes with narrow ones such as selected sites, remove knowledge sources and actions the agent does not need, and apply Conditional Access.
Microsoft 365 admin center

The **agents** page in the Microsoft 365 admin center lists every agent, pending publish requests, ownerless agents and at risk agents. Admins can install, **block** for the organisation, delete (restorable for 30 days), assign a new owner and approve publishing. AI Administrator approves requests and assigns owners.

check.q: A Brightwater agent has read and write access to every mailbox through an application permission, but only needs one shared mailbox. How should Tomasi reduce its blast radius?
options: Add a sponsor who checks it monthly
Give it a sensitivity labelled knowledge source
Block it in the Microsoft 365 admin center
Replace it with a narrowly scoped permission
check.why: Narrowing permissions directly shrinks what a compromised agent could reach while keeping it working. A sponsor adds accountability but not less access, a labelled source does not limit mailbox rights, and blocking stops the agent entirely.

lessons.key: Agent blast radius is permissions plus knowledge plus capabilities, shown in Defender's AI agents inventory, and managed through narrow scopes and the Microsoft 365 agents page.

lessons.title: AI gateway in API Management for Foundry
steps: Why a gateway

If apps call model endpoints directly, keys are shared, one app can use all the tokens and nobody sees consumption. The **AI gateway** in Azure API Management sits in front of Microsoft Foundry endpoints and fixes all three.
Adding it

From Foundry, Tomasi adds an AI gateway to the Foundry resource, either creating a new API Management instance (Basic v2, for dev and test) or choosing an existing v2 instance. Microsoft recommends Standard v2 or Premium v2 for production. There is one gateway per Foundry resource, shared by its projects.
Token controls

**Token limits** cap tokens per minute per project, returning 429 when exceeded, and total token **quotas** return 403. Token metrics flow to Azure Monitor, a content safety policy checks prompts, and semantic caching reuses similar answers.
Identity

The gateway authenticates to the model back end with a **managed identity**, so client apps never hold model keys. Brightwater gives the customer claims assistant a token limit so a sudden traffic spike cannot exhaust capacity for the staff tools.

check.q: Brightwater's customer chatbot keeps using up the model capacity shared with internal tools. What should Tomasi configure in the AI gateway?
options: A content safety policy on prompts
A per project tokens per minute limit
A semantic cache for repeated answers
A token metrics policy to Azure Monitor
check.why: Token limits cap each project's consumption, returning 429 when exceeded, so one app cannot starve the others. Content safety, caching and metrics are useful AI gateway policies but do not cap usage.

lessons.key: The AI gateway in API Management fronts Foundry with token limits, quotas, monitoring, content safety and managed identity access to models.

lessons.title: Defender for AI Services and Foundry guardrails
steps: Defender for AI Services

**Defender for AI Services** is a Defender for Cloud plan enabled per subscription by an Owner or Contributor. It watches Azure OpenAI and Foundry model deployments and detects jailbreak attempts flagged by Prompt Shields, sensitive data leakage, credential theft and suspicious access. Alerts correlate into Defender XDR incidents.
Plan settings

**User prompt evidence** includes the suspicious parts of prompts and responses in alerts, with sensitive data redacted. **Data security for AI interactions** lets Purview classify and govern prompts. **AI model security** scans models in Azure Machine Learning registries for malware and unsafe serialisation.
Foundry guardrails

**Guardrails** detect risks such as hate, sexual, self harm and violence content (each with a severity threshold), user prompt attacks, **indirect attacks** hidden in documents or tool output, protected material, personal information and task drift. They apply at **user input** and **output**, and for agents also at **tool call** and **tool response**, with actions to annotate or annotate and block.
Inheritance

An agent with no guardrail inherits its model deployment's guardrail. An agent with its own guardrail uses only that one. Brightwater's claims assistant reads customer uploaded documents, so Tomasi adds an indirect attack control on tool responses set to annotate and block.

check.q: Brightwater's Foundry agent reads customer documents through a grounding tool, and Tomasi fears hidden instructions inside them. Which guardrail setting fits?
options: A violence threshold set to low on user input
Indirect attack control on tool response, blocking
A user prompt attack control set to annotate
PII detection on the agent's output
check.why: Instructions hidden in retrieved documents arrive in the tool response, so an indirect attack control there with blocking addresses it. Input side controls do not see tool output, annotate only does not block, and PII detection targets personal data.

lessons.key: Defender for AI Services detects attacks on model deployments, and Foundry guardrails filter inputs, outputs and agent tool traffic, including indirect attacks.

lessons.title: The Data and AI security dashboard
steps: One view of data and AI

The **Data and AI security dashboard** in Defender for Cloud groups resources into storage, managed databases, hosted databases and AI services, and shows whether each is fully, partly or not protected by the relevant plans.
Top issues
It highlights the most severe alerts by MITRE tactic, critical and high recommendations, and attack paths that end at data or AI resources.
Closer looks

The data view shows sensitive data discovered, data threat alerts and explorer queries such as public storage holding sensitive data. The AI view shows **AI discovery**, AI threat protection results and queries such as sensitive data used for grounding and internet exposed resources used for grounding.
Getting the full picture

A complete dashboard needs Defender CSPM with sensitive data discovery, Defender for Storage, Defender for Databases and the AI services plan, with each subscription registered for the Microsoft Security provider. Tomasi uses it to spot a storage account holding claim documents that grounds the assistant and is reachable from the internet.

check.q: Parts of Brightwater's Data and AI security dashboard are empty. What is the most likely cause?
options: Purge protection is off on Key Vaults
Subscriptions lack the needed Defender plans
The dashboard only works in Sentinel
check.why: The dashboard draws on several Defender plans, and sections stay empty without them. The number of resources, Sentinel and purge protection do not control what it shows.

lessons.key: The Data and AI security dashboard shows protection coverage, top risks and AI grounding exposure, and needs the relevant Defender plans enabled.

lessons.title: Disk encryption and Trusted launch
steps: Disk encryption options

**Server side encryption** is always on for managed disks with platform keys, or your own keys through a **disk encryption set**, but does not cover temp disks or caches. **Encryption at host** encrypts temp disks, caches and data in transit to storage, and Microsoft recommends it for new VMs.
Azure Disk Encryption

**Azure Disk Encryption** encrypts inside the guest using BitLocker or DM-Crypt with keys in Key Vault. Microsoft has announced it retires in September 2028, so Brightwater plans to move to encryption at host.
Trusted launch

A VM's **security type** is set at creation: standard, **Trusted launch** (Generation 2 VMs, the default for new ones) or confidential. **Secure Boot** allows only signed boot components, blocking bootkits. A **vTPM** stores keys and measures the boot chain.
Integrity monitoring and confidential VMs

**Boot integrity monitoring** uses Secure Boot, the vTPM and the guest attestation extension, and Defender for Cloud alerts when attestation fails. **Confidential VMs** add hardware memory encryption and can bind OS disk encryption to the vTPM. Existing Generation 1 VMs can be upgraded to Trusted launch.
